title: Electrolyte Replacement Calculator 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
description: Calculate sodium, potassium & fluid needs per hour of exercise based on weight, duration, temperature & intensity. Free 2026 sports hydration tool.
intro:
Every endurance athlete who has hit the wall, cramped at mile 18, or felt dizzy after a long summer ride has experienced electrolyte depletion firsthand. The problem isn't just dehydration — it's the invisible loss of sodium, potassium, and other minerals dissolved in your sweat that quietly destabilize muscle function, nerve signaling, and cardiovascular output long before thirst kicks in.

Sweat rates in humans vary enormously: research published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism documents individual sodium losses ranging from as low as 230 mg per liter to over 1,700 mg per liter, a nearly 7-fold difference between athletes of similar size running at the same pace. That variability is why generic advice like "drink 8 glasses a day" or "have a sports drink" can leave serious athletes dangerously under- or over-corrected.

This calculator combines four of the most influential variables in sports hydration science — your body weight, total exercise duration, ambient temperature, and exercise intensity — to produce personalized hourly targets for sodium, potassium, and fluid intake. Weight matters because larger bodies produce more sweat in absolute terms. Duration matters because electrolyte deficits compound over time; what's tolerable at 60 minutes becomes critical at 180. Temperature matters because heat accelerates sweat rate non-linearly — moving from 15 °C to 35 °C can double sweat loss. Intensity matters because higher cardiovascular demand increases both core temperature and sweat rate independently of the environment.

The output gives you actionable hourly targets — not vague "drink more" guidance — so you can build a concrete race-day or training-day nutrition plan. Whether you're a recreational cyclist tackling your first century ride, a competitive triathlete dialing in an IRONMAN nutrition strategy, a trail runner preparing for a mountain 50K, or a sports dietitian building client protocols, the numbers this tool generates give you a defensible, evidence-based starting point.

One important caveat: this calculator uses population-level reference values drawn from exercise physiology research. Your personal sweat composition, acclimatization status, heat adaptation, fitness level, and medication use all introduce individual variation. Use these outputs as a structured first estimate, then refine them through sweat testing, perceived exertion monitoring, and — when in doubt — consultation with a sports medicine physician or registered sports dietitian.
keyTakeaway: Formula: **mg per hour of exercise**. Direct application with your input values. Calculate sodium, potassium, and fluid replacement for long-duration athletic activity.

useCases.title: Marathon Runner in Hot Weather
useCases.description: A 70 kg runner races a road marathon (4.5 hours) in 28 °C heat at moderate-high intensity. The calculator estimates a sodium need of roughly 550–700 mg/hour, totaling ~2,750–3,150 mg across the event, and a fluid target near 650–750 mL/hour. Armed with this, the athlete plans to carry two salt capsules (each ~250 mg sodium) per aid station and supplement a standard sports drink, rather than relying on the drink alone.

useCases.title: IRONMAN Triathlete Pre-Race Planning
useCases.description: An 80 kg triathlete competing in a 10–11 hour IRONMAN in 22 °C conditions uses the calculator to model separate bike and run segments at different intensities. The bike leg (5 hours, moderate intensity) yields a target of ~500 mg sodium/hour and 600 mL/hour fluid. The run leg (5.5 hours, moderate intensity) bumps to ~600 mg/hour due to accumulated heat stress. Total sodium need: ~5,800 mg. This informs a custom bottle mix with additional electrolyte tabs.

useCases.title: Trail Ultramarathon with Temperature Swing
useCases.description: A 65 kg ultrarunner faces a 100-mile mountain race starting at 8 °C overnight, peaking at 30 °C midday. Running two separate calculations — one for the cool overnight segment and one for the hot afternoon — reveals sodium needs nearly doubling in the heat phase (from ~380 mg/hour to ~720 mg/hour). The runner packs a graduated supplement strategy: light electrolyte drink at night, salt tabs plus electrolyte mix during the hot hours.

useCases.title: Recreational Cyclist on a Century Ride
useCases.description: A 85 kg recreational cyclist plans a 6-hour century (100-mile) ride in 20 °C weather at low-moderate intensity. The calculator suggests ~480 mg sodium/hour and 550 mL/hour fluid. At 6 hours, total needs: ~2,900 mg sodium and ~3.3 liters fluid. The cyclist realizes a single standard bidon (500 mL) per hour of plain water and a banana won't cover sodium needs, and adds a commercial electrolyte mix to every other bottle.

useCases.title: Sports Dietitian Building a Client Protocol
useCases.description: A registered dietitian uses the calculator to generate a baseline hydration protocol for a 58 kg female soccer player who plays two 90-minute matches per weekend in summer (30 °C, high intensity). The calculator outputs ~700 mg sodium/hour and 700 mL/hour fluid. This becomes the starting framework for a sweat-testing referral and iterative protocol refinement, replacing the club's generic "drink a sports drink at halftime" advice.

useCases.title: Exercise Physiology Students Comparing Scenarios
useCases.description: A university class uses the calculator to illustrate how a single variable change alters electrolyte recommendations. Students run the same 75 kg athlete at identical intensity for 2 hours, varying only temperature from 10 °C to 40 °C in steps. They observe sodium recommendations climb from approximately 420 mg/hour to 760 mg/hour, providing a concrete, quantified demonstration of heat's non-linear effect on sweat physiology — a concept often stated but rarely shown numerically in textbooks.

useCases.title: High-Intensity CrossFit or HIIT Athlete
useCases.description: A 90 kg male CrossFit competitor completes daily double sessions (2 × 1.5 hours) in a poorly ventilated gym at an effective temperature of 27 °C. Running two separate calculations reveals a daily sodium need exceeding 2,400 mg from exercise alone — before accounting for basal dietary needs. Seeing the number helps the athlete understand why afternoon cramping persists despite feeling "well-hydrated" from drinking plain water, and motivates a switch to an electrolyte-fortified intra-workout drink.

useCases.title: Cold-Weather Nordic Skier
useCases.description: A 72 kg Nordic skier competes in a 3-hour cross-country race at −5 °C but at very high intensity. Many athletes assume cold eliminates electrolyte concerns. The calculator shows that high-intensity output at −5 °C still requires ~400 mg sodium/hour and ~500 mL fluid/hour — less than summer conditions, but significant. Cold-blunted thirst and the inconvenience of carrying bottles make this group particularly prone to under-fueling, and the output quantifies what's at stake.

explanation:
**Normal reference values in sports** come from large population studies and sports science research. They vary by age, sex, fitness level, and climate. These are guidelines; your personal medical history and individual tolerance always take priority.

## How It's Calculated

During extended exercise, you lose electrolytes through sweat. This calculator applies the formula based on your inputs and typical ranges for your exercise profile.

The calculation considers:
- Body weight and sweat rate
- Exercise duration and intensity
- Environmental temperature
- Standard electrolyte replacement recommendations

## Normal Reference Ranges for Athletes

| Parameter | Typical Range |
|---|---|
| Sodium loss in sweat | 400–800 mg/hour |
| Potassium loss in sweat | 100–200 mg/hour |
| Fluid intake | 500–750 mL/hour |
| Blood sodium (normal) | 135–145 mEq/L |
| Blood potassium (normal) | 3.5–5.0 mEq/L |
| Max fluid per hour | 1,000–1,200 mL |

## Final Notes

This calculator is a reference tool. For critical decisions—especially if you have a medical condition, take medications, or have a family history of metabolic disorders—consult a sports medicine physician or registered dietitian. Values are current for 2026 and reviewed periodically.

faq.q: Why is electrolyte replacement more important than just drinking water during prolonged exercise?
faq.a: Water alone dilutes blood sodium concentration when consumed in large amounts during exercise, a condition called exercise-associated hyponatremia (EAH). EAH can cause nausea, swelling, confusion, and in severe cases, cerebral edema and death. The 2015 Consensus Statement from the Third International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Development Conference documented EAH fatalities in previously healthy athletes who drank only water. Sodium co-ingested with fluid maintains plasma osmolality, drives intestinal water absorption via sodium-glucose co-transporters, and preserves the thirst signal. Potassium is similarly lost in sweat and is critical for muscle membrane repolarization after each contraction — depletion contributes to cramping, weakness, and cardiac arrhythmia risk. Replacing electrolytes isn't just performance optimization; in multi-hour events it's a safety necessity.

faq.q: How do I know if my sweat rate is higher or lower than average?
faq.a: The gold-standard field method is the pre/post exercise weight method: weigh yourself (in the nude) immediately before and after a 1-hour training session, making note of any fluid consumed during that hour. Every kilogram of body weight lost equals approximately 1 liter of sweat. A 70 kg runner who loses 1.2 kg in one hour (and drank 400 mL) has a sweat rate of roughly 1,600 mL/hour — above the typical 800–1,400 mL/hour range. For sodium specifically, commercial sweat patch testing (Nix Biosensor, Precision Hydration sweat testing) or laboratory iontophoresis can quantify sodium concentration in your sweat. High sweat sodium is often hereditary — you may notice white salt stains on your kit or skin after training, a reliable informal indicator that you're a 'salty sweater' who needs above-average sodium replacement.

faq.q: What is the physiological basis for adjusting electrolyte needs by temperature?
faq.a: Core body temperature rises during exercise. To dissipate heat, the hypothalamus signals eccrine sweat glands to increase secretion — a process regulated by sympathetic cholinergic nerves. Sweat rate increases roughly proportionally with ambient heat load plus metabolic heat production. Research from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute shows that at 33 °C versus 20 °C, sweat rates in trained cyclists can increase by 40–80% even at identical power outputs. Because sweat is a sodium-rich fluid (~20–80 mmol/L sodium), absolute sodium losses rise proportionally with sweat volume. Additionally, acclimatization to heat over 10–14 days improves sweat efficiency — acclimatized athletes produce more sweat but at a lower sodium concentration — meaning sodium needs per liter of sweat decrease with heat adaptation, though total losses can still rise due to higher sweat volume.

faq.q: How does exercise intensity specifically affect electrolyte requirements?
faq.a: Intensity determines metabolic heat production. At higher intensities, more ATP is hydrolyzed per unit time, more heat is generated, and sweat rate increases even in cool conditions. A runner at race pace (e.g., lactate threshold intensity) can have a sweat rate 50–100% higher than the same runner at an easy jogging pace at the same temperature. Additionally, high-intensity exercise shifts the body toward greater reliance on anaerobic glycolysis, increasing lactate and hydrogen ion production. This alters intracellular and extracellular fluid composition differently than aerobic exercise. For practical purposes: low-intensity exercise (hiking, easy riding) in mild weather needs the least electrolyte support; high-intensity exercise in heat requires maximum replacement and the shortest interval between intake doses to prevent cumulative deficit.

faq.q: Can I drink too much during exercise — and how would I know?
faq.a: Yes. Overdrinking during exercise is one of the leading causes of EAH. The outdated 'drink ahead of thirst' doctrine — promoted in the 1990s — has since been refuted by research from Dr. Timothy Noakes and others. Current consensus from the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM 2023 position stand) recommends drinking to thirst as the primary guide, with personalized pre-calculated targets (like those from this calculator) as a secondary check. Signs you may be overdrinking include: weight gain during a race (you should maintain weight or lose a small amount), bloating, nausea without other cause, and puffiness in hands or face. Urine color is a useful field check: very pale yellow to clear during exercise may indicate over-hydration; amber to dark yellow indicates underhydration. Target a light lemonade color.

faq.q: Are there differences in electrolyte needs between male and female athletes?
faq.a: Yes, with some nuance. On average, male athletes have higher absolute sweat rates due to greater body mass, higher metabolic rates, and more active sweat glands — meaning total sodium losses are often higher in men. However, sweat sodium concentration (mg per liter of sweat) doesn't differ consistently by sex in research. Female athletes tend to have lower sweat rates per unit body surface area, meaning relative electrolyte needs scale with body weight more tightly. Hormonal cycling also matters: luteal phase (post-ovulation) increases body temperature set point slightly, potentially increasing sweat rate and electrolyte needs in the second half of the menstrual cycle. Female athletes should also be aware that they appear more susceptible to EAH in some studies, possibly due to differences in anti-diuretic hormone sensitivity and smaller body size. Adjusting intake by weight (which this calculator does) accounts for much of the sex difference.

faq.q: What foods and drinks provide the most practical electrolyte replacement during and after events?
faq.a: During exercise: commercial sports drinks (Gatorade Endurance ~620 mg sodium/L, Skratch Labs ~380 mg/L, Precision Hydration PH 1500 ~1,500 mg/L) offer graded sodium replacement; salt capsules (SaltStick ~215 mg each) add sodium without calories; electrolyte chews and gels with sodium are convenient for running. Real food options mid-race: pickles (a 30 mL shot contains ~200–500 mg sodium), pretzels (~500 mg/oz), and broth (~900 mg sodium per cup) are popular at ultras. Post-exercise: chocolate milk (electrolytes + carbs + protein), tomato juice (high sodium), bananas (potassium-rich), and salted nuts provide broad-spectrum replenishment. The key for post-exercise recovery is sodium-first — sodium drives both thirst and fluid retention, so eating salty food after exercise before or with fluids improves rehydration efficiency compared to drinking plain water.

faq.q: What is hyponatremia and how is it different from ordinary dehydration?
faq.a: Hyponatremia is defined as blood sodium below 135 mmol/L (normal: 135–145 mmol/L), caused during exercise primarily by excessive hypotonic fluid intake that dilutes plasma sodium. Dehydration, by contrast, involves total fluid deficit — elevated blood sodium and osmolality. The conditions are physiologically opposite, yet their early symptoms (nausea, fatigue, headache) overlap significantly, making field differentiation difficult. The critical distinction: a dehydrated athlete improves rapidly with fluid intake; a hyponatremic athlete worsens with more plain water. Symptomatic hyponatremia (below ~125 mmol/L) causes cerebral edema, seizures, and can be fatal within hours. First aid for severe EAH involves small boluses of hypertonic saline (3% NaCl, ~100 mL IV), a hospital emergency intervention. Preventive strategy — not overdrinking, ensuring electrolyte co-ingestion — is far more effective than treatment. This calculator helps quantify the sodium needed to keep plasma concentration stable.

faq.q: Should I use this calculator differently for training versus racing?
faq.a: Yes. Race day and training days call for different strategies. In training, you can tolerate mild fluid and electrolyte deficits as a controlled stress that builds adaptation (particularly for heat acclimatization and gut training to absorb electrolyte solutions). Many coaches deliberately restrict fluids slightly in training to force adaptation. For racing, especially events over 2 hours, you want to arrive at the start line well-hydrated, execute a pre-calculated intake plan from the first 30 minutes (don't wait until you feel thirsty or depleted), and adjust in real time based on conditions. Use this calculator in training to establish your personal baseline, then validate it with pre/post weight checks and performance feedback before relying on the numbers in competition. Also consider that race-day adrenaline and pace increases mean you'll likely sweat more than in equivalent training efforts.

faq.q: Are there medications or health conditions that change electrolyte replacement needs significantly?
faq.a: Yes — several common conditions and medications substantially alter electrolyte physiology. Hypertension medications including thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) and loop diuretics (furosemide) cause baseline urinary sodium and potassium losses, meaning athletes on these medications may start exercise already depleted. ACE inhibitors and ARBs can alter potassium handling. NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) reduce renal sodium excretion and increase EAH risk — their use during ultra-endurance events is now actively discouraged by race medical directors. Athletes with kidney disease have impaired ability to excrete excess sodium or potassium, making both over- and under-replacement dangerous. Cystic fibrosis dramatically elevates sweat sodium concentration (often 3–5× average), requiring substantially higher sodium replacement. Addison's disease impairs aldosterone production, increasing sodium losses. Any athlete with a chronic condition, or who takes daily prescription medications, should consult a physician or sports medicine specialist before using population-level electrolyte targets — including those from this calculator.

faq.q: How does gut tolerance limit electrolyte intake, and what can I do about it?
faq.a: Even when your sweat losses demand high sodium and fluid intake, your gastrointestinal tract has absorptive limits that vary significantly between individuals. High-intensity exercise reduces gut blood flow by 50–80% as blood is preferentially directed to working muscles and skin. This slows gastric emptying and increases intestinal permeability ('leaky gut'), causing nausea, bloating, and diarrhea when intake exceeds absorptive capacity. Practical limits for most athletes: gastric emptying rate caps around 800–1,000 mL/hour of fluid during moderate-high intensity exercise. Carbohydrate concentration above ~8% slows gastric emptying (isotonic sports drinks are typically 6%). For sodium specifically, very high concentrations can cause GI distress without adequate fluid volume to buffer them. Gut training — systematically consuming sports nutrition products during training at race-representative intensities over weeks to months — measurably improves gut tolerance through enhanced transporter upregulation and motility adaptation. Start implementing your race-day hydration strategy in training at least 8–12 weeks before the event.

faq.q: What's the role of potassium specifically, and do most athletes actually need to supplement it?
faq.a: Potassium is the dominant intracellular cation, with ~98% of total body potassium stored inside cells. It plays a critical role in muscle membrane potential, nerve conduction, and cardiac rhythm regulation. Sweat contains potassium, but at much lower concentrations than sodium: typically 4–8 mmol/L potassium versus 20–80 mmol/L sodium. For most athletes in events under 4–5 hours, dietary potassium from food (bananas, potatoes, avocados, legumes) consumed before and after exercise is sufficient. Significant potassium depletion requiring supplementation during exercise is more relevant in ultra-endurance events (12+ hours) or when athletes have restricted diets. The more common potassium problem is the post-exercise depletion window: intense exercise drives potassium out of muscle cells into plasma temporarily (raising blood potassium acutely), but after exercise, potassium shifts back intracellularly, sometimes lowering plasma potassium and contributing to post-race cramping and fatigue. Eating a potassium-rich meal within 2 hours of finishing resolves this for most athletes. Athletes with cardiac arrhythmia history or on diuretics should have potassium levels monitored by a physician.
